cards.headline: Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin criticize Western policies ahead of trilateral meeting with Donald Trump

pages.text: Chinese leader Xi Jinping pledged to stand up against trade protectionism while Russian President Vladimir Putin criticized Western sanctions during speeches at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, China. The leaders' remarks set the stage for a trilateral meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump, scheduled for November 19, 2026, on the sidelines of the summit. The three leaders of the world's largest nuclear powers may discuss the war in Ukraine, the war in Iran, trade, artificial intelligence, and nuclear weapons.

The upcoming meeting follows a shift in U.S. strategy; Jonathan Czin, a former CIA China expert at the Brookings Institution, noted that the administration has moved 180 degrees from previously identifying China and Russia as principal geopolitical competitors. Czin suggested the meeting's subtext might be more significant than its substance, as U.S. allies in Asia and Europe may perceive the Trump administration as prioritizing accommodation of China and Russia over countering their influence. Czin also described the gathering as a potential 'political coup' for Putin, who could share the international stage despite Western isolation.

While President Trump stated he intends to raise the war in Ukraine with Xi and Putin, administration officials have said the conflict will not be part of the discussions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern regarding major powers discussing global spheres of influence without Ukraine present. Regarding trade, Jia Hui Tee, a senior trade policy analyst at the Hinrich Foundation, noted that Trump and Xi could potentially make progress on reciprocal tariff cuts covering goods worth $30 billion on each side, though a timeline has not been set. Experts interviewed by DW do not expect breakthroughs on technology or other issues, suggesting the leaders may instead focus on maintaining the existing trade truce.

cards.headline: Kuwait and Bahrain repel Iranian drone attacks following US strikes on Qeshm Island

pages.text: Kuwait and Bahrain reported repelling Iranian air attacks on November 17, 2026, as hostilities between Iran and the United States intensified. The drone attack on Kuwait was the first such incident in more than two months. Kuwait's military stated its air defenses engaged drone threats but reported no casualties or damage. The Iranian army claimed it had targeted the Ali Al Salem Airbase in Kuwait, which hosts US forces, though Kuwaiti authorities did not report any damage from the attempt. The Kuwaiti foreign ministry condemned the attack, stating it flagrantly violated the country's sovereignty and constituted a grave breach of international law. In Bahrain, air defenses intercepted attacks from Iran, following a claim by Tehran’s Revolutionary Guard that it had attacked a base in the country used by Washington. Bahrain and US Central Command (CENTCOM) stated the drones were intercepted without damage.

The aerial attacks followed US warplane strikes on an Iranian missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. US military officials confirmed the strikes were in retaliation for Iran's targeting of US personnel and assets. On Qeshm Island, Iranian news agency IRNA reported hearing five to six explosions in the city, while the semi-official Fars news agency reported explosions and smoke billowing northwest of the city. Ahmad Nafisi, the deputy governor of Hormozgan, told IRNA that the strikes did not cause damage to residential or commercial districts and that the situation was under control. Additionally, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed it shot down a US MQ-1 Predator reconnaissance and combat drone in southern waters near Qeshm Island, alleging it used a new advanced air defense system to destroy the drone at 13:45 local time. The IRGC stated this was the eighteenth drone of that type its forces have destroyed.

The escalation occurs within a nine-month-old war that began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February. Since then, Iran has retaliated by launching missiles and drones at Israel and Gulf Arab states hosting US military assets. Tensions have also centered on the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway through which approximately one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments pass. Iran has attempted to restrict traffic in the strait, insisting ships use only authorized routes. US officials noted the recent airstrikes followed incidents in which at least five ships hit naval mines while sailing through what Iran calls unauthorized routes. Separately, the United Arab Emirates' state oil firm reported that a crew member was missing after one of its tankers was attacked in the Gulf waterway on November 17, 2026.

cards.headline: Palestinian woman shot dead by Israeli settlers near Jericho, witnesses say

pages.text: A 72-year-old Palestinian woman, Fadha Wadha, was shot dead in an overnight attack by Israeli settlers in the village of al-Duyuk al-Tahta in the West Bank, according to resident testimonies. Wadha was standing outside her home when she was struck in the head by a bullet as settlers fired toward Palestinian houses, residents reported to the Guardian. The attack occurred in a village where dozens of Israeli settlers, some armed, moved into eight buildings two weeks ago with the support of the settler organization Nachala and a regional council representing illegal settlements in the central West Bank.

Abu Younis, a cousin of Wadha’s husband, told the Guardian that the violence began when a group of settlers attacked a young boy they accused of entering a courtyard seized from Palestinian residents. Younis stated that approximately 15 settlers in several vehicles chased the boy and began firing indiscriminately. Witnesses said that as Palestinian residents began throwing stones to defend themselves, more settlers arrived and shot at civilians, injuring six men. Wadha’s son, Arafat Fidhat, was also wounded by gunfire. His wife, Naama Fidhat, told Reuters that Arafat was wounded in the torso after he rushed to the scene and accidentally collided with a parked settler vehicle that witnesses said was empty at the time. Naama Fidhat further stated that while Arafat was being taken to a hospital in Ramallah, Israeli soldiers stopped the ambulance and arrested him.

cards.headline: Israeli tanks advance into central Gaza as military targets Hamas infrastructure

pages.text: Israeli tanks have advanced into the central Gaza Strip, with witnesses reporting vehicles moving onto the main Salahudeen road. The Israeli military stated its forces are conducting an operation to target Hamas infrastructure west of the Yellow Line, a boundary established by an October 2025 ceasefire that separates Israeli-controlled territory from Hamas-controlled areas in the enclave. COGAT, an Israeli military body responsible for civilian matters in the Palestinian territories, warned Palestinian civilians and international aid agencies to avoid areas near the Al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps and the Salah al-Din road. An Israeli military spokesperson said the operation is targeting Hamas infrastructure and noted that the military had also struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier. Israel has stated it is stepping up attacks because Hamas has been regrouping and rearming, while Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the US-brokered ceasefire agreement.

Palestinian medics reported that one person was killed in an Israeli airstrike near the army raid in central Gaza. Medics also stated that separate Israeli airstrikes killed two other people earlier in the day in Deir Al-Balah and Gaza City. The military spokesperson had no immediate comment on the other strikes. The current fighting occurs despite an October 2025 ceasefire that halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war but has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured the disarmament of Hamas. Gaza health authorities report that at least 1,600 Palestinians have been killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while the Israeli military says 5 Israeli soldiers have been killed. Palestinian authorities state that more than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign launched after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel during an attack on October 7, 2023.

The military operation unfolds as Palestinians face severe shortages of food and shelter. On November 17, 2026, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the UN's World Food Programme (WFP) warned that access restrictions and funding shortfalls put many Palestinian lives at risk. Currently, more than 1.7 million Gazans are displaced; the IOM and WFP report that 1.4 million face acute hunger and 1.98 million require shelter assistance. With Gaza's infrastructure decimated, more than 80% of Palestinians are unemployed. WFP Palestine Country Director Shaun Hughes stated that families in Gaza are facing their first sleepless nights of a long winter ahead.

cards.headline: Ethiopia and Eritrea amass forces along shared border

pages.text: Ethiopia and Eritrea have amassed forces along their shared border, according to conflict monitors and individuals tied to militias in northern Ethiopia’s Tigray region. The build-up has brought the two armies within striking distance of each other, according to the conflict monitors ACLED and International Crisis Group, a person close to a pro-Ethiopian government militia in Tigray, and a person close to anti-government rebels in the region. These developments have fueled fears of outright war between the historical rivals, who previously fought a border war from 1998 to 2000 that killed tens of thousands of people over a dispute regarding the town of Badme. ACLED stated on November 17, 2026, that artillery shelling and armed clashes have occurred near Badme as Ethiopia’s military moved to clear Tigrayan rebels from near the border.

Conflicting reports exist regarding recent combat between the two nations. ACLED and a person close to the rebels stated that the two sides clashed in recent days, which would mark their first direct armed exchanges in over a month. However, a person close to the pro-Ethiopian government militia in Tigray disputed that clashes occurred. Reuters could not independently confirm reports of skirmishes between Ethiopian and Eritrean forces along the border. Regarding the military build-up, Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel decried “propaganda” from Ethiopia’s ruling party but did not directly address reports of military build-ups or clashes. Spokespeople for the Ethiopian government did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Tensions have risen since fighting broke out in September between Ethiopia’s federal government and rebels in Tigray, a region that borders Eritrea. Witnesses and the Ethiopian government said Eritrean forces crossed into Tigray in early October in support of the rebels. ACLED reported that drone strikes, which it believed were carried out by Ethiopia’s military, targeted those Eritrean troops, though Ethiopia has not commented on the strikes. Eritrea has denied any incursion into Ethiopia and accused Addis Ababa of seeking a pretext to invade. The two nations are separated by a border stretching more than 1,000 km (620 miles).

cards.headline: Israel postpones construction contracts for West Bank E1 settlement

pages.text: Israel has postponed issuing contracts for the construction of a large settlement in the West Bank, an expansion known as E1. The delay follows the imposition of sanctions by the United Kingdom against eight construction firms operating in the area on November 16, 2026. The E1 expansion involves land between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim, a West Bank settlement city of nearly 40,000 residents. The development is considered qualitatively different because the land bisects the West Bank and cuts it off from East Jerusalem; UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband stated the expansion would mark the death knell of a future Palestinian state.

Israeli attorney general Gali Baharav-Miara ordered the Israel land authority and the ministry of housing not to open the tender process for the settlement. Baharav-Miara stated that any decision regarding settlement expansion should not be taken by the caretaker government led by Benjamin Netanyahu, but rather by a new administration. While Israeli diplomats insisted the postponement was not a response to the measures from Downing Street, they suggested that UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband had acted prematurely in sanctioning the firms. Conversely, UK diplomats believe growing political pressure on Israel over settlements, including from US Democrats, is having an impact.

The E1 settlement expansion was due to have been announced on November 12, 2026. The deferral places the expansion as a factor in upcoming coalition negotiations. Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the Change bloc and a figure seen as Israel’s most likely next prime minister, has opposed the E1 expansion, describing it as a mistake that could alienate international opinion. Eisenkot noted that Netanyahu had previously opposed the plan but approved it due to coalition pressure. Matan Kahana, the newly elected Knesset speaker and an ally of Eisenkot, has also expressed opposition to violent settler activity.

cards.headline: Bangladesh Prime Minister brands Awami League a terrorist group

pages.text: Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has branded the Awami League a terrorist group and called for the organization to be crushed before it can rise again. Speaking during his concluding speech at the fourth session of the Jatiya Sangsad, Rahman stated that the group, whose activities are currently banned, is not a political party but a terrorist group that has repeatedly engaged in terrorist activities both at home and abroad in Bangladesh. He called for the group to be resisted in the spirit of the 2024 mass uprising.

During a 38-minute address, Rahman alleged that the Awami League has engaged in killing, enforced disappearances, and torture. He claimed the group's fugitive leader instructed supporters to set fire to the homes of pro-democracy individuals and issued orders to prepare lists of democracy supporters for targeted killings, noting that these instructions were circulated on social media. Rahman also cited a barbaric attack on a Bangladeshi female artiste in Italy and attempts to humiliate National Citizen Party (NCP) Convener Nahid Islam as recent examples of the group's activities.

Rahman stated that the group's actions challenge politics itself and cannot be tolerated. He also addressed those he accused of attempting to destabilize Bangladesh by sheltering and patronizing the group, suggesting they prioritize ties with terrorists over the people of Bangladesh. Rahman concluded by referencing the 1971 Liberation War and the 2024 mass uprising, asserting that patriotic people did not fight to accept subservience to others.

cards.headline: Tunisia’s olive oil export revenues reach record 5.2 billion dinars

pages.text: Tunisia’s olive oil export revenues rose 39 percent to a record 5.2 billion dinars ($1.71 billion) during the 2025-2026 season, according to the National Observatory of Agriculture (ONAGRI). This increase follows a record olive oil harvest of approximately 500,000 tons in the same season, which established Tunisia as the world’s second-largest olive oil producer after Spain. The bumper crop drove export volumes up 47.5 percent to around 413,100 metric tons. As Tunisia's leading agricultural export and a major source of foreign currency, these revenues provide a boost to an economy facing high public debt, weak growth, and limited access to international financing.

During the first 11 months of the 2025-2026 season, Tunisian olive oil reached 85 countries. The European Union remains the country's largest export destination, though North America has emerged as an important market. While international demand is strong, the country faces challenges in capturing higher value from its production; approximately 84.3 percent of exports were shipped in bulk, while bottled and packaged oil accounted for just 15.7 percent of volumes.

cards.headline: More than 220 people jailed in Guinea crackdown on illegal gold mining

pages.text: Authorities in Guinea have sentenced more than 220 people to prison as part of a crackdown on illegal gold mining, a campaign that has triggered deadly clashes and mass displacement. In Conakry, a court handed two-year sentences to 22 former local officials for their roles in water pollution and environmental destruction. Additionally, 202 miners were jailed for three years for environmental offences and illegal mining. Among those sentenced, foreign nationals have been banned from Guinea for 10 years. While illegal gold mining has provided a livelihood for hundreds of thousands of people in Guinea, authorities state the operation is intended to protect rivers and farmland from the toxic chemicals and heavy machinery used in the process.

The crackdown has resulted in violence in the northeast of the country, where protests against mining restrictions left 10 people dead and 13 others injured. The consequences of the enforcement are also affecting the region's borders, as tens of thousands of miners and their families have fled into neighboring Mali.

cards.headline: United States and Iran engage in pattern of limited confrontation in Middle East

pages.text: The United States and Iran have entered a period of intermittent attacks and economic pressure, avoiding full-blown military confrontation since a June Memorandum of Understanding between the two sides fell apart in July. This pattern of limited confrontation, which analysts say could continue for months without escalating into all-out war, involves both nations using military and economic levers to inflict pain on the other side. Both countries have maintained blockades in and around the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway that was once the conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies. Recent military actions include an air strike by the United States on Iran’s Qeshm island on November 17, 2026, and claims by Iran that it has targeted US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait. Meanwhile, Iran has continued to target ships it says have not followed its rules for passing through the Strait of Hormuz, while the US maintains economic sanctions and a naval blockade of Iran’s ports.

Sustaining this status quo involves mounting economic and political costs that analysts suggest could become untenable for either side, particularly Iran. Hamidreza Azizi, a senior Iran analyst at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that the two sides have different calculations regarding the costs of prolonging the confrontation. Azizi noted that as economic pressure mounts, Iran may become increasingly willing to take military risks to break the deadlock, potentially deciding that an escalating confrontation is preferable to the current status quo. In the United States, the administration of President Donald Trump has appeared to shift gears on Iran following the Republican Party's defeat by the Democratic Party in midterm elections. Both Trump and Vice President JD Vance have acknowledged that the deeply unpopular Iran war was partly to blame for that election outcome.

cards.headline: Democrat Mary Peltola unseats Republican Dan S. Sullivan in Alaska Senate race

pages.text: Democrat Mary Peltola won the US Senate seat in Alaska on November 17, 2026, defeating incumbent Republican Senator Dan S. Sullivan. Peltola received 144,302 votes, while Sullivan received 131,844 votes. Even if the 4,760 votes earned by a second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan were combined with Sullivan's total, Peltola would have still won. This victory completes a sweeping midterm election win for the Democratic Party, which also won back the House of Representatives and secured a 56-44 majority in the US Senate. This result gives Democrats control of the US Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump's presidency. Peltola is the first Alaska Native elected to the US Senate and the first Democrat to win a US Senate seat in Alaska since 2008. In a victory statement, Peltola said the status quo in Washington, D.C. is not working for Alaska and pledged to fight corporate greed and lower costs for working families. She noted that in rural Alaska, she has spoken to parents choosing between heating homes and buying food, and to elders regarding empty fish racks.

The Alaska election was marked by controversy and legal challenges. A New York Times investigation reported that aides to Peltola worked with individuals who attempted to recruit so-called spoiler candidates—candidates intended to confuse voters by siphoning votes from an opponent—in an alleged attempt to mislead Alaskans. Peltola has denied having any knowledge of the alleged plot. During the race, Donald Trump called for the 6,105 votes won by Republican candidate Gerald Heikes to be immediately given to Sullivan as a fair solution, but merging those votes would not have been enough to overcome Peltola's lead. Trump also characterized the presence of two candidates named Dan Sullivan as a Democratic use of a decoy. The Trump administration personally ordered a legal bid to ask courts to block the certification of the results if Sullivan lost due to the potential name confusion, though a federal judge dismissed that bid before the election. Additionally, US Attorney Michael Heyman claimed federal investigators were conducting both criminal and civil probes involving the Alaska Senate race. The official count took two full weeks to complete following the November 3 poll due to the logistical challenges of collecting ballots from Alaska's remote expanse.

cards.headline: Deliberate denial of humanitarian aid to children in conflict zones has increased 16-fold in a decade

pages.text: An analysis by Save the Children shows that the deliberate withholding of humanitarian aid from children in conflict zones has increased 16-fold over the last decade. The assessment of UN-verified incidents indicates that the “weaponisation” of aid—the practice of restricting access to vital assistance—is becoming a normalized tactic of modern warfare. According to the data, proven cases where children were denied access to humanitarian aid rose from 509 in 2015 to 8,322. This shift is reflected in UN records, where more than a fifth of all violations against children in conflict now involve the denial of aid, compared to 2% a decade ago.

Most incidents of aid restriction identified in the analysis occurred in Palestine. On November 15, 2026, the UK, Australia, Canada, and Italy urged Israel to allow critical aid into Gaza to assist displaced people living in flimsy shelters during the first heavy winter rains. During these storms in the besieged territory, an infant drowned and three children and a mother were killed. The request for aid comes as Israel refuses to allow 150,000 tents and other vital supplies past its border controls.

cards.headline: Iraq approves rehabilitation of oil pipeline to Türkiye as flows resume after 12 years

pages.text: Iraq has resumed pumping crude oil for export through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline to Türkiye, following the completion of technical and operational tests. On November 17, 2026, Iraq’s Cabinet approved a recommendation to rehabilitate the pipeline, hours after the resumption of flows was announced. The pipeline connects Iraq's northern oil-producing region to Türkiye’s Mediterranean port of Ceyhan and had been out of service since 2014 following repeated attacks by the terrorist group ISIS (Daesh). This reopening provides Baghdad with an additional export outlet, reducing its dependence on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a waterway where Iraq has been impacted by competing blockades from the US and Iran. Oil revenue from sales contributes to 90 percent of Iraq's budget.

Oil Minister Basim Mohammed Khudair stated that flows began at 120,000 barrels per day (bpd) and are expected to gradually rise to 500,000 bpd, though he provided no timeline for reaching that level. The Kirkuk pipeline has a capacity of more than 1.5 million bpd. The Cabinet decision was made during a meeting in the southern province of Najaf chaired by Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi. The Cabinet approved a recommendation from the Ministerial Council for the Economy regarding the rehabilitation, though the statement from the Prime Minister's media office did not detail the specific provisions or the work involved. The Ministerial Council for the Economy also reviewed the ministry's crude export plan and instructed the ministry to intensify export efforts.

The resumption of Kirkuk exports is part of broader regional energy movements. In August, Iraq and Türkiye signed a one-year agreement to maintain oil flows through the Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline, providing for a transportation capacity of up to 750,000 bpd while the two countries pursue a long-term arrangement. Additionally, in September 2025, Iraq began reexporting oil to Türkiye from the semiautonomous Kurdistan region following a two-year dispute, with the Kurdistan regional government and foreign producers agreeing to allow 180,000 to 190,000 bpd to flow to Ceyhan. While the new announcement allows oil from Iraq's federal government to flow directly to Ceyhan, Baghdad also seeks to connect Basra, its southern energy hub, to the Mediterranean via the Syrian port of Baniyas and Türkiye's port of Ceyhan.

cards.headline: Acting US Navy Secretary acknowledges Iran war is putting strain on maritime forces

pages.text: United States Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao testified before the Senate Armed Services Committee that the war between Israel and Iran is taxing the maritime service. During his confirmation hearing for the permanent top civilian role, Cao acknowledged the conflict is a strain on the navy, though he maintained that joint military efforts have “really set China back on their heels.” The war has now entered its ninth month. Senators from both parties questioned Cao regarding the human and material costs of the conflict, specifically citing extended ship deployments, dwindling weapons stockpiles, and the shifting of resources away from the Asia-Pacific region.

The hearing occurred amid political fallout from the protracted war in the Middle East. A recent attempt in the US House to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth over his management of the war failed. Additionally, the November midterm elections, which were widely viewed as a repudiation of the war and its economic impact, resulted in Republicans losing control of both the House and the Senate. The Democratic-controlled 120th Congress is scheduled to be sworn in on January 3, 2027. During the nearly two-hour hearing, Senator Jack Reed of Rhode Island, the ranking Democrat on the committee, expressed concern regarding Cao's leadership record as acting secretary. Reed also pressed Cao on whether he would protect military leaders from partisan interference following Hegseth's ongoing and planned dismissals of numerous naval officers over the past year.

Democratic lawmakers also criticized the US Navy for failing to provide standard congressional notification after it quietly relieved the entire leadership team of the nuclear-powered attack submarine USS South Dakota. The leadership team, consisting of the commander, executive officer, and command master chief, was relieved following an October underwater collision with the seabed. Cao, a retired US Navy captain and former Republican candidate for the Virginia Senate, has served as acting navy secretary since April 2026 after previously serving as under-secretary. He is currently seeking Senate confirmation for the permanent position and is backed by US President Donald Trump.

cards.headline: Ghana receives 6.57 million forest carbon credits, becoming first African nation under ART TREES program

pages.text: Ghana has been issued 6.57 million carbon credits for reducing greenhouse gas emissions from deforestation and forest degradation. The credits, issued to the Government of Ghana on November 12, 2026, under the Architecture for REDD+ Transactions (ART) program, make Ghana the first country in Africa to receive credits through this framework. The government expects to receive approximately US$43 million from the sale of some of these credits. These credits recognize forest protection efforts across approximately 2.5 million hectares conducted between 2017 and 2021 under Ghana's Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation (REDD+) programme. REDD+ is a framework designed to cover forest conservation, sustainable forest management, and efforts to increase the amount of carbon stored in forests.

Ghana is also the first country to receive credits under ART's TREES Crediting Level approach, which carries the Core Carbon Principles (CCP) Approved label from the Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market (ICVCM). The issuance follows years of work to improve forest monitoring and reduce activities that cause forest loss, such as illegal mining, logging, and agricultural expansion. In some areas, cocoa production has also contributed to forest loss as farms expand into forest landscapes. Ghana's programme involves government agencies, cocoa farmers, private companies, and local communities working to address these pressures and support sustainable agricultural practices. The credits provide an opportunity for Ghana to raise funds for forest protection and to support farmers and communities that depend on forest resources for their livelihoods.

cards.headline: Hotels on Grand Canyon's South Rim to reopen as park eases water restrictions

pages.text: Officials at Grand Canyon National Park in Arizona have announced they are easing water restrictions, allowing hotels on the South Rim to once again accommodate overnight guests. The El Tovar Hotel and several other lodges will reopen following a milestone in the restoration of water service. While lodging is returning, park officials stated that food and beverage services will resume gradually. Park officials are also urging visitors to conserve water, such as by taking shorter showers and turning off faucets when not in use, as restoration of the water system continues.

The restoration follows severe flooding in late August that caused three deaths, prompted rescues, and damaged key infrastructure. The damage included a water intake pump and a significant stretch of a decades-old pipeline that supplies water to millions of visitors at the South Rim and approximately 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village. Although officials previously expected to be just over a month away from completing a more than $200 million upgrade to the 12.5-mile-long (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline, additional flooding in September damaged temporary repairs.

cards.headline: Turkey increases diplomatic pressure over integration of Kurdish-led forces in Syria

pages.text: Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan met with US envoy Tom Barrack in Ankara as Turkey increased its diplomacy regarding Syria. The meeting occurred amid concerns from Ankara that the integration of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) into Syrian state institutions is lagging. Turkey views the SDF as a threat to its national security. Neither Fidan nor Barrack disclosed the contents of their discussion, according to the Turkish Foreign Ministry. Barrack serves as the US ambassador to Turkey and the special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq.

The meeting between Fidan and Barrack followed a visit to Ankara on November 17, 2026, by Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani and Defense Minister Murhaf Abu Qasra. During that visit, the two Syrian officials met with Fidan and Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler, and Shibani also held talks with Barrack. cards.headline: Mysterious radio signals may originate from dead stars

pages.text: Astronomer Scott Hyman and his colleagues have identified a curious source of radio waves that may be produced by the dense remains of dead stars, such as neutron stars or white dwarfs. While examining archived observations from the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa taken in May 2022, the team discovered signals with unusual properties that differ from previous mysterious bursts detected decades ago. These signals are classified as long-period radio transients, which are sources that produce bursts of radio waves at intervals ranging from minutes to hours.

The discovery follows a separate mystery first identified in 2002, when Hyman and his colleagues detected five mysterious bursts of radio waves near the center of our galaxy. Those specific signals were spaced roughly 77 minutes apart. While those bursts were detected again in 2003 and 2004, they subsequently disappeared, and scientists found no sign of their return despite years of searching. The 2022 observations of long-period radio transients represent a different type of signal that may offer clues to their origins.

cards.headline: CPD proposes Tk 24,204 living wage for Bangladesh garment workers

pages.text: The Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD) recommended a living wage of Tk 24,204 for garment workers in Bangladesh on November 18, 2026, to cover food, housing, and other essentials while allowing for modest savings. The think tank suggested that negotiations for a new minimum wage should take place within a range of Tk 18,578 to Tk 24,204. This proposal follows ongoing labor unrest in industrial zones such as Ashulia, Savar, and Gazipur, where protests have led to factory closures and clashes with police. The current minimum wage is Tk 12,500. The CPD's proposed range is intended to address the gap between the current wage and the costs required to keep a four-member family, with 1.58 earners, above the upper poverty line or at a standard living wage level.

The CPD's calculations identified three specific benchmarks for the Ready-Made Garment (RMG) sector. First, an inflation-adjusted wage of Tk 16,351 was identified as the amount needed to purchase the same goods and services as before, though the CPD noted this would add nothing in real terms. Second, Tk 18,578 was estimated as the minimum needed to keep a family of four above the upper poverty line. Third, Tk 24,204 was identified as a standard living wage. During a press conference in Dhaka, CPD Executive Director Dr. Nazneen Ahmed stated that policy should gradually transition workers toward a living wage through discussions between parties rather than open-ended bargaining. CPD Distinguished Fellow Dr. Debapriya Bhattacharya criticized a lack of fiscal transparency, noting that the government has not placed quarterly economic statements before parliament as required by the Public Money and Budget Management Act 2009.

The proposal arrives as a government-formed Minimum Wage Board attempts to resolve industry instability. On November 18, 2026, the board had already received a proposal from workers' representatives seeking Tk 48,000 for grade one, Tk 43,000 for grade two, Tk 38,000 for grade three, Tk 32,000 for grade four, and Tk 30,000 for apprentices. Factory owners' representatives are expected to submit a counter-proposal at a board meeting on November 23. The CPD flagged institutional deficits in the board, noting it is operating without reliable data on living costs or factory capacity to pay. To prevent future unrest, the CPD recommended establishing a permanent wage commission for annual inflation-linked reviews and making the wage revision cycle legally binding, suggesting the schedule for revisions be announced at least six months in advance.

cards.headline: Indigenous Ngäbe communities in Panama fear a second dam as damage from the first remains unrepaired

pages.text: Indigenous Ngäbe communities in western Panama are facing the potential construction of a second dam on the Changuinola River after a report found that the first hydroelectric project continues to cause severe environmental, cultural, and spiritual harm. Panamanian authorities have granted a concession for this second dam while local communities continue to seek reparations for the impacts of the CHAN-75 hydroelectric dam project. According to a report by the Indigenous rights organization Cultural Survival, the Ngäbe people still suffer from displacement, pollution, the loss of medicinal plants, the loss of local fish species, and threats to their livelihoods and spiritual practices.

Ismael Quintero, a Ngäbe leader of the Guayabal community, stated that lives changed completely when the state-owned electric power generation company Empresa de Generación Eléctrica (EGESA) began building the first dam in 2007. Quintero told Mongabay that before construction, crops were abundant and there was free navigation along the Changuinola River, which his family described as clean and healthy. For the Ngäbe, the river is sacred and holds deep spiritual significance; they believe a spirit resides within the river as the owner of the fish and ecosystems, and they offer prayers to this spirit before undertaking activities there. Quintero noted the river provides food, such as shrimp and fish, and serves as a source of strength and inspiration.

cards.headline: Study finds AI misidentifies wildlife species and suggests incorrect geographic ranges

pages.text: A study published in the Biodiversity Data Journal suggests that general-purpose artificial intelligence may not be ready for conservation work due to errors in species identification. Researchers evaluated OpenAI's GPT-5.2 using 10,000 research-grade iNaturalist photographs of vertebrate species recorded in Colombia, including 2,000 images each of amphibians, birds, fishes, mammals, and reptiles. The study found that AI errors can lead to incorrect species names or suggest animals are located outside their natural ranges, which could affect how researchers interpret species distributions and cause the presence of rare animals to go unnoticed, according to study author Gustavo Nicolas Paez Salamanca.

One error involved a small marsupial, Metachirus myosuros, photographed by a camera trap in the Morrocoy protected areas in Montes de María, Colombia, where the conservation organization Sembrandopaz monitors wildlife. Despite being told the animal was seen in Colombia, the AI identified it as Bassariscus sumichrasti, a species whose known range does not include the country. An expert confirmed the correct identification of Metachirus myosuros. Other errors identified in the fieldwork included the AI assigning an older, superseded name to the porcupine Coendou vossi, a species recognized as distinct only in 2025, and issues involving the armadillo Cabassous centralis, which has been known to science for decades but has few publicly available verified photographs.

cards.headline: Ontario proposes increasing minimum fines for excessive vehicle noise to $200

pages.text: Ontario is proposing to increase the minimum fine for excessive vehicle noise from $60 to $200. Transportation Minister Prabmeet Sarkaria announced the proposed changes to the Highway Traffic Act at a news conference, stating the government is responding to requests from residents, municipalities, and police services for harsher penalties to act as a stronger deterrent. While the minimum fine would rise, the maximum fine would remain at $1,000.

The Highway Traffic Act currently requires vehicles to have mufflers in a good working order to prevent excessive smoke and unusual noise, and it prohibits drivers from causing unnecessary vehicle noises. However, the Act does not provide specific details regarding permitted sound levels or the specific types of noise that are prohibited. Police in Ontario currently have the authority to issue fines for noise caused by engine revving, speeding, and prohibited exhaust modifications.

Peel police Deputy Chief Mark Andrews said the proposed tougher penalties would support existing enforcement efforts against a small group of people who disturb tens of thousands of residents. Andrews noted that Peel police have laid over 5,000 charges for excessive vehicle noise since 2024, describing the issue as a recurring community concern. He stated that officers continue to see individuals modify exhaust systems, stunt drive, and treat roads like race tracks.

cards.headline: Conservationists tag 10 large eels to track migration in River Tees catchment

pages.text: Conservationists working on the Eels of Steel project have captured and electronically tagged 10 large eels to monitor their migration through the River Tees catchment. The project, which is funded by Natural England and conducted by the Tees Rivers Trust alongside Hull University, aims to determine if the critically endangered European eels can successfully navigate river barriers like weirs and sluices as they migrate toward the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda. The team used fyke netting—a method involving a cylindrical net—to find 12 large eels during the summer and autumn, though they only managed to tag 10 of them. The largest eel caught measured 60cm (23in) in length and weighed 435g (0.9lbs). Project manager Ellie Ward noted that the eels caught were harder to catch and not as large as usual. Ward suggested that low river flows during the summer, which have continued into autumn, may have contributed to these low catch rates.

cards.headline: Ghana's public debt reaches GH¢759.3 billion as cedi loses 10.6% against US dollar

pages.text: Ghana's public debt stock reached GH¢759.3 billion in October 2026, according to the Bank of Ghana's November 2026 Summary of Economic and Financial Data. This represents an increase of GH¢23.5 billion in the three months leading up to October. During the same period, the cedi lost 10.6 per cent of its value against the US dollar. The debt-to-GDP ratio rose to 47.5 per cent in October, up from 46.1 per cent in July. Measured in US dollars, the debt burden grew to US$65.3 billion from US$63.4 billion in July, driven by borrowing and exchange rate movements.

The trajectory of the nominal debt stock was uneven throughout the year. After a marginal dip to GH¢732.1 billion in August, the debt rose sharply to GH¢756.8 billion in September and reached GH¢759.3 billion in October, adding GH¢27.2 billion in those two months. This follows a steady accumulation from GH¢663.4 billion in January to GH¢720.8 billion by May. In July, external debt was US$28.5 billion, representing 20.7 per cent of GDP, while domestic debt stood at GH¢427.9 billion in October, or 26.8 per cent of GDP.

Fiscal indicators show a tightening public purse. The government recorded a cash deficit of 2.3 per cent of GDP in July. The primary balance, which is the government's budget balance after stripping out interest payments, posted a surplus of 0.1 per cent of GDP in October, a decrease from the 1 per cent surplus recorded in July. Regarding currency performance, the cedi traded at GH¢11.69 to the dollar in November. The cedi also fell 9.2 per cent against the pound to GH¢15.47 and 5 per cent against the euro to GH¢12.92 on the interbank market.

cards.headline: Digital content consumption increasingly correlates with political leanings, study finds

pages.text: Researchers have found that digital consumption habits, including social media use, are increasingly linked to how citizens vote. A study presented at the 2026 ACM Internet Measurement Conference in Karlsruhe, Germany, suggests that app usage provides data on vote distribution across municipalities that traditional socioeconomic indicators, such as income, age, and unemployment, do not capture alone. The research, titled “Digital Consumption and Political Alignment: Evidence from Mobile Data Across Two European Elections in France,” was conducted by researchers from IMDEA Networks, Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, Northeastern University, and Orange Research.

To analyze these patterns, researchers examined 4,102 urban and suburban localities in France during the 2019 and 2024 elections. They compared two predictive models for each political party: one based on traditional socioeconomic factors and another that incorporated app usage data. Adding digital information improved the correlation between estimated vote shares and actual election results by an average of around 10% in 2019 and 28% in 2024 across parties.

The analysis identified specific differences between individual applications. Facebook was associated with higher percentages of votes for the Rassemblement National (RN), a French far-right party, in both the 2019 and 2024 elections. Additionally, Facebook use was associated with lower percentages of votes for other parties, most notably for La France Insoumise (LFI) in 2024.

cards.headline: Manitoba diagnostic scan wait times reach record highs

pages.text: The number of Manitobans waiting for common diagnostic scans has reached record levels, with doctors and patients stating the crisis puts lives at risk. According to provincial diagnostic wait time data, the number of people waiting for CT scans and ultrasounds now exceeds the wait times seen during the COVID-19 pandemic. These scans are used to help diagnose potentially deadly medical conditions, including heart disease and brain tumours. Dr. Fourie Smith, a family physician who has practised in Manitoba since 1998, said the situation is worse now than it has ever been.

Provincial data shows significant increases in waitlists compared to 2019, the earliest year for which publicly available data exists. As of August 2026, over 45,000 people were waiting for an ultrasound, compared to an average of 16,000 in 2019. Almost 29,000 people were waiting for a CT scan in August, up from 8,000 in 2019, while 18,000 were waiting for an MRI, up from 15,000 in 2019.

Winnipeg comedian Big Daddy Tazz sought private care after being told he would likely wait a year for a spine MRI, a test that creates images of structures inside the body. To avoid potential further damage while waiting for a diagnosis for pain in his arms and legs, he paid $950 for a private MRI in Kelowna, B.C., where he has a second home. The test revealed a pinched nerve tunnel in his spine and a condition putting pressure on his spinal cord. While he does not require surgery, the results provided a path for pain management through exercise and stretches.

cards.headline: Dead Melbourne Cup racehorse found in Sydney waste facility

pages.text: The body of So You Are, an Australian thoroughbred that finished eighth in the Melbourne Cup, was discovered at an industrial waste facility in Sydney after being dumped. A member of the public, Gregg Jowett, found the horse and posted a video of the discovery to social media, stating, “That can't be normal. Does anyone know if that's legal?” and “I'm disgusted by that.”

Trainer Bjorn Baker announced on November 16, 2026, that So You Are died following a “severe bout of colic.” Baker stated the horse was rushed to a specialist equine hospital for emergency veterinary treatment but could not be saved. Following the discovery of the remains, Baker said he was “deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains,” adding that the horse deserved to be treated with dignity and respect. Baker noted that the REC Equine Specialists veterinary practice had launched an investigation into the incident.

REC Equine Specialists apologized for the “distress” caused by the footage, stating that So You Are should have been “promptly and respectfully buried.” The practice explained that the horse had been euthanised under anaesthesia before being collected by a “contracted provider” and taken to a “licensed landfill.” The company said what happened was “unacceptable and disrespectful” and announced it had stopped using the provider “effective immediately.”

cards.headline: Mississauga mayor prepares to fight legal appeals against data centre moratorium

pages.text: Mississauga Mayor Alvin Tedjo said he is prepared to fight two companies challenging the city's decision to block a data centre project at the Ontario Land Tribunal. Tedjo, in his first one-on-one interview since his inauguration, told CBC News, “I say, bring it on,” regarding the legal challenges to the city's one-year moratorium on certain data centre developments. The mayor stated that Mississauga residents have been clear that they do not want American real estate investment trusts determining what is built in their communities. The moratorium, passed unanimously by Mississauga city council in September, uses an interim control bylaw to freeze data centre projects for one year. This pause allows the city to study potential impacts on energy, water, and noise before establishing permanent regulations or guardrails.

The legal challenges involve U.S.-based Prologis and Toronto-based Montcrest. On Nov. 4, Prologis launched a tribunal appeal against the decision. Prologis had been pursuing a 40-megawatt facility on Tenth Line in the city's northwest, located south of Highway 401 near an Ikea warehouse and an electrical substation. Prologis spokesperson Mattie Sorrentino said multiple companies have filed appeals due to concerns regarding a “lack of a clear planning rationale” and “sweeping restrictions.” Sorrentino stated the bylaw is “poorly conceived without justification for its restrictions or consideration of the consequences for businesses seeking to invest in Mississauga,” adding that the restriction creates uncertainty and delays investment. Montcrest's notice of appeal cites the moratorium's impact on the “potential future use” of its Tahoe Centre land near Dixon Road and Eglinton Avenue, south of Toronto Pearson Airport. Montcrest did not respond to questions regarding whether the site was intended for a data centre or if it had active applications for the energy grid.

The Mississauga bylaw applies to data centres with energy demands exceeding 10 megawatts, which is approximately enough electricity to power 10,000 homes. Mississauga is the largest of at least six Ontario municipalities to enact a similar pause in recent months. City councillor Martin Reid, who championed the moratorium, stated, “The fight is not done,” and “We can never put development before planning.” The moratorium can be extended for a second year as officials study grid strain and land-use impacts. The appeals could test the ability of municipalities to use temporary bans to regulate the wave of projects driven by the artificial intelligence boom.

cards.headline: Portrait paintings from 1650 to 1950 show shifting female beauty ideals

pages.text: Research published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences suggests that preferences for less curvaceous female body shapes emerged centuries before the influence of modern mass media like movies or social media. By analyzing approximately 300 years of portraits, researchers found that depictions of women tended to move toward straighter figures with less pronounced waists in relation to their hips in later paintings. This study challenges the common assumption that the emphasis on slim figures and reduced curves is a phenomenon shaped primarily by the last century of media influence.

Jeanne Bovet of Northumbria University in the U.K. and colleagues conducted the study using 486 paintings of wealthy women drawn from three major online art collections. To analyze these works, more than 1,500 participants were divided into three groups to assess 606 depictions of upper-class women. One group assessed body shapes by comparing the painted women to nine silhouettes representing different body weights and waist-to-hip ratios to find the closest match. A second group rated attractiveness and estimated whether the women had previously given birth, while a third group estimated the women's ages based on their faces. The researchers then examined how these assessments changed over the 300-year period, accounting for factors such as perceived age and body weight.

cards.headline: Newfoundland judge denies bail to man accused of intimate partner violence

pages.text: A Newfoundland judge denied bail to Zachary Dunphy, an accused offender who allegedly boasted about the ease of obtaining release in Canada. Justice Vikas Khaladkar issued the decision on Nov. 4, citing the federal Bail and Sentencing Reform Act to deny Dunphy's application to the Supreme Court of Newfoundland and Labrador. This follows a previous denial of bail at the provincial court level in May and a subsequent application in October. Dunphy has pleaded not guilty to a dozen charges, including forcible confinement, assault with a weapon, choking, dangerous operation of a motor vehicle, and failure to comply with a probation order. He is scheduled for trial in March.

The denial of bail was influenced by the Bail and Sentencing Reform Act, which came into effect in July. This federal law makes it more difficult for certain offenders, including repeat violent offenders, to obtain release. Under these rules, the legal burden shifts: instead of the Crown having to prove why an accused person should remain in custody, the onus is on the offender to prove why they should be released. Justice Khaladkar applied this to Dunphy due to the violent nature of the alleged offences and his criminal history. In his decision, Khaladkar addressed Dunphy's alleged views on Canadian law, writing, “Not anymore,” and stating that the Act is intended to stop instances where persons released on bail inflict grievous bodily harm and death on intimate partners.

The charges against Dunphy stem from an incident in which he allegedly followed his former girlfriend into a restaurant washroom, dragged her out by her hair, and held her at knifepoint before fleeing at speeds up to 150 km/h. It is alleged that in the aftermath, Dunphy texted the complainant’s sister, saying: “I’ll get bail. This is Canada. She’ll be with me by the end of the day.” Justice Khaladkar noted that the legal landscape has changed, stating, “This is no longer the Canada that gave recidivist offenders the benefit of the doubt because of the presumption of innocence.”

cards.headline: Winter rains deepen Gaza shelter, sanitation, and food security crisis

pages.text: Winter rains in Gaza are flooding makeshift shelters and destroying scarce food supplies, leaving more than 1.7 million displaced people struggling to stay warm and fed, according to United Nations agencies. Karl Baker, the regional crisis coordinator for the UN International Organization for Migration (IOM), stated that tens of thousands of shelters were damaged or destroyed after just one day of rain. The flooding and sewage have also destroyed food stocks stored in tents, while cooking gas and firewood remain unavailable or unaffordable. Humanitarian partners reported that two children died in fires accidentally started by families attempting to stay warm by cooking inside their tents, and at least five people were killed by a collapsed sand bank just over a week ago.

The World Food Programme (WFP) is facing significant challenges in providing nutrition to the population. Shaun Hughes, the WFP country director for Palestine, noted that most people burn rubbish to cook food, but the rain has left the rubbish wet. Hughes, briefing journalists in Geneva following a visit to the Strip, stated that in tented camps for displaced families, the WFP previously provided one hot meal a day, but now provides one hot meal every two days. Currently, 1.4 million Gazans face acute hunger. The UN's food and migration agencies warned that recent improvements in food security are precarious and sustained mainly by humanitarian aid rather than recovery in local markets or food systems, and that winter flooding risks reversing those gains.

The humanitarian response is under pressure from critical funding shortfalls and continued restrictions on humanitarian aid deliveries. The UN agencies warned that these factors are adding pressure to an already fragile response as displaced families face the winter months. The combination of destroyed food stocks, lack of fuel, and damaged shelter has increased fears regarding how the displaced population will withstand the upcoming winter.

cards.headline: Pregnenolone may alter communication between brain regions linked to depression

pages.text: Researchers at UT Southwestern Medical Center and UT Dallas have found evidence that pregnenolone, a naturally occurring steroid hormone produced from cholesterol, may alter patterns of communication between key brain regions involved in depression and cognitive control. The study, published in the Journal of Clinical Psychiatry, suggests the hormone could change functional connectivity—the way different parts of the brain work together—in ways that might inform future depression treatments. This research could lead to the development of neuroimaging biomarkers, which are brain-based markers used to observe how neurosteroids affect neural circuits in patients.

The study was a double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial involving 29 women with mild to moderate major depressive disorder. Participants underwent three different seven-day treatment conditions: receiving 500 milligrams (mg) of oral pregnenolone, 800 mg of oral pregnenolone, or a placebo. Researchers used serum samples and functional MRI (fMRI) exams to conduct testing. fMRI is a brain-imaging technique that allows researchers to study brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow and oxygen levels. E. Sherwood Brown, M.D., Ph.D., M.B.A., a Professor of Psychiatry in the Peter O’Donnell Jr. Brain Institute at UT Southwestern and the study's corresponding author, noted that while previous studies suggested pregnenolone might treat depression in people with bipolar disorder, researchers previously lacked insight into how it affects neural circuits specifically involved in depression.

cards.headline: Ontario bill would prevent lawsuits against government over OSAP pause

pages.text: The Ontario government has introduced Bill 148, an omnibus bill that has passed its first reading and includes provisions to prevent legal action against government officials regarding a provincewide pause on Ontario Student Assistance Program (OSAP) payments to students at private post-secondary institutions. Under the proposed legislation, legal action could not be launched against officials for financial damages, neglect, or default under the Ministry of Training, Colleges and Universities Act. The bill would also eliminate lawsuits against the government resulting from fraud investigations, enforcement actions, registration suspensions, or decisions involving the Training Completion Assurance Fund, a program designed to protect students if a career college ceases operations. Ontario NDP Leader Marit Stiles challenged the legislation in Queen's Park, alleging the province is prioritizing protection from lawsuits over resolving the situation caused by the OSAP pause for career college students. Stiles characterized the legislation as retroactive.

Ontario's colleges and universities minister, Nolan Quinn, defended the OSAP freeze for students at career colleges. Quinn stated that the government is holding institutions accountable and that the legislation would make those institutions liable for the misuse of OSAP across the private career college system. During question period, Stiles stated that Quinn has not provided a dollar figure regarding the amount of money provided to what she termed 'scam' colleges and argued that the government lacks a plan to make students whole or fix OSAP.

cards.headline: Drug that mimics Viagra may slow Alzheimer’s progression by 31%

pages.text: A global stage three trial suggests that AR1001, a pill that mimics the mechanism of Viagra, can slow cognitive decline in people with early Alzheimer’s disease by 31%. The findings were presented at the Clinical Trials on Alzheimer’s Disease conference in Boston. AR1001 is a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, a type of medicine that relaxes blood vessels to increase blood flow. While Viagra is used to treat erectile dysfunction, researchers found this drug may work by boosting blood flow to the brain and likely stimulating brain cell pathways that promote learning and memory. The South Korean company AriBio, which manufactures AR1001, reported that the drug slowed decline in 604 people who were taking no other drugs for Alzheimer’s. However, in a wider group of patients who were taking other drugs, the tablet did not achieve statistically significant results.

The trial spanned 13 countries, including the UK. Experts not involved with the study described the results as “exciting” and “very promising,” noting they could signal a “totally new treatment” for the condition. Prof Tara Spires-Jones, a professor of neurodegeneration at the University of Edinburgh and a fellow at the Academy of Medical Sciences, said the results looked “very promising.” Dr Sheona Scales, director of research at Alzheimer’s Research UK, called the findings “very encouraging” and an “important milestone in the search for new Alzheimer’s treatments.” Alzheimer’s is the most common form of dementia, a condition currently without a cure that is forecast to affect 153 million people worldwide by 2050.

cards.headline: Florida fungus found to contain both psychedelic compounds and deadly toxins

pages.text: The fungus *Galerina indica*, dubbed the “dark magic mushroom,” is the first species known to contain both mind-altering psychedelic chemicals and deadly toxins. Found in the wetlands of central Florida, the small brown mushroom produces the psychedelic compounds psilocybin and psilocin, alongside deadly amatoxins. While some mushrooms are known to contain either psilocybin or amatoxins, this discovery represents a rare convergence of both chemical properties in a single species. Findings regarding the fungus were published in the journal *Current Biology* on November 11.

Andrew Kunik, a fungal biologist at the University of Florida and study co-author, identified the species on a moss-covered palm trunk while studying fungi in central Florida in 2025. Kunik noted that the specimen turned blue when handled, which can be a sign of psilocybin production. To investigate, Kunik and colleagues performed chemical analyses on *G. indica* and specimens of two unnamed *Galerina* species collected in the southeastern United States between January 2024 and September 2025. The analysis confirmed that *G. indica* contained psilocybin, psilocin, and two amatoxins, including one toxin that had never been documented in mushrooms before.
